The recovery in Chinese seaborne crude oil imports has stalled month-to-date (Aug 1-15 data), per @Vortexa. China imported an average of ~6.8m b/d in the first two weeks of the month, down from ~7.3m b/d in July. 

Tanker arrivals suggest, however, an uptick in the second half of Aug, but smaller than initially anticipated. For now, China is keeping seaborne buying well below pre-war level.
For the 2nd day in a row, that was a rather interesting North Sea crude window. Oil flat price is up, time-spreads and physical differentials down.

BRENT’s six-month calendar spread is trading in a backwardation of just under $10 per barrel implying traders see crude supplies relatively restricted in the short term. The spread has eased from a recent high of nearly $19 in late July but is still much tighter than the small contango reported at the start of last month before the ceasefire between the United States and Iran broke down. From an empirical perspective, the spread is consistent with some tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz but flows remaining far below normal and where they were when the ceasefire was in effect:

The market has yet to realize that there is no TACO for Trump. 

Scenario 1: the US leaves the region and Iran is in control

Let’s assume that Trump decides that this war is too much, and he wants to leave the region. He folds completely, agrees to withdraw all of the troops, and hands Iran control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran will immediately turn around, continue to use the Strait of Hormuz as leverage, and demand concessions from Israel. You see, to become a regional hegemon means that you need to eliminate all threats.

Israel, which sees the conflict with Iran as all-or-nothing (similar to how Iran sees the conflict with the US), will just escalate, which will force the US back into the fold. Israel could threaten to bomb Iran’s energy infrastructure, which would force Iran to retaliate against GCC energy infrastructure creating a permanently higher plateau for oil prices because of structural losses in production capacity.

This means that scenario 1 is not even a plausible path to pursue. Iran will escalate even if the US capitulates, and Israel will force the US to re-enter down the road.

Lose-lose.
